findings: ELEVENLABS AGENTS (formerly Conversational AI) — Transports: primary realtime transport is a WebSocket API at wss://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/convai/conversation?agent_id={agent_id} (public agents use agent_id directly; private agents use a server-minted signed URL via /v1/convai/conversation/get-signed-url) — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/libraries/web-sockets . Additional transports per the platform overview: SIP trunking, Twilio/Vonage/Telnyx/Plivo/Bandwidth/Sinch telephony connectors, native iOS (Swift), Android (Kotlin) and React Native SDKs, a React SDK/embeddable widget, and a low-level WebSocket API for custom integrations — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/overview . A WebRTC path exists but is brokered: the client-events docs note that 'Over WebRTC connections, the audio event is not sent as audio is handled directly by LiveKit' — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/events/client-events.md .

ELEVENLABS — Turn detection / VAD / interruption: the architecture is 4 components — a fine-tuned ASR model, your choice of LLM (or a custom LLM), a TTS model, and 'a proprietary turn-taking model that handles conversation timing' — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/overview . Configurable knobs (all under conversation_config): turn.turn_timeout 'take turn after silence' 1-30s; turn.turn_eagerness patient|normal|eager; conversation.max_duration_seconds (default 600s); turn.soft_timeout_config (filler phrase while the LLM thinks, disabled by default); and interruptions enable/disable via the client_events list — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/conversation-flow . The client is streamed a vad_score event (0..1 'probability the user is speaking') and an agent_response_correction event that carries the truncated agent text after an interruption — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/events/client-events.md . No documented way to replace the turn-taking model itself.

ELEVENLABS — Tools / function calling: five tool kinds — Client tools (run in the browser/mobile app), Webhook tools (LLM generates query/path/body params against an external API, with custom headers/auth connections), Code tools (custom JavaScript executed in a sandbox on ElevenLabs infrastructure), MCP tools (Model Context Protocol servers), and System tools (end_call, transfer_to_number, transfer_to_agent, skip_turn, play DTMF, voicemail detection, update_state, language detection, flag-for-review) — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/tools and https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/tools/webhook-tools.md . Webhook tools are configured with name/description/method/URL ({} path params), headers, auth, body schema, and can write dynamic variables back from the response — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/tools/webhook-tools.md . Post-call webhooks exist for end-of-call + analysis — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/overview .

ELEVENLABS — Session state / context: conversation history is stored server-side (there is a full Conversations API: list/get/summaries/audio, plus text and semantic search over history) — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/overview and https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/quickstart . Per-conversation personalization uses dynamic variables and overrides; the client-to-server events 'contextual_update' and 'user_message' inject extra context mid-conversation without interrupting the flow, and 'user_activity' signals suppress agent interrupts — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/events/client-to-server-events.md . Agent transfer preserves the full transcript across the handoff (see below).

ELEVENLABS — Transcript / realtime event schema (JSON over the WebSocket): server-to-client events include conversation_initiation_metadata {conversation_id, agent_output_audio_format, user_input_audio_format}; ping; audio {audio_base_64, event_id, alignment{chars, char_durations_ms, char_start_times_ms}}; user_transcript (finalised utterance); agent_response; agent_response_correction {original_agent_response, corrected_agent_response} (truncation after interruption); agent_response_metadata (custom LLM only); client_tool_call {tool_name, tool_call_id, parameters} with a client_tool_result reply; agent_tool_response / agent_tool_response_full_payload (64KB truncation); agent_chat_response_part {type: start|delta|stop, text, event_id} for streaming text; vad_score; mcp_tool_call {state: loading|awaiting_approval|success|failure}; agent_response_complete; guardrail_triggered — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/events/client-events.md . Note: only finalised user transcripts are documented as an event (no user partial/interim event), whereas agent text can stream via agent_chat_response_part.

ELEVENLABS — Agent handoff / multi-agent: the transfer_to_agent system tool transfers an in-progress conversation to another agent; transfers can be nested (Orchestrator -> Agent 1/2/3 -> Agent 2a); the LLM calls transfer_to_agent with {reason, agent_number} (zero-indexed into configured transfer rules that map a natural-language condition to a target agent_id, with delay_ms, transfer_message, enable_transferred_agent_first_message) — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/tools/system-tools/agent-transfer.md . On transfer the parent overwrites the child's client events and TTS/ASR audio formats (and carries the current language); everything else (prompt, voice, tools, turn/timeout settings) is the child's; the full transcript is preserved and the transfer tool call is STRIPPED from the child's visible history; post-call evaluation sees the full unfiltered transcript but individual messages carry no agent_id, so the transfer tool call acts as the boundary marker — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/tools/system-tools/agent-transfer.md .

ELEVENLABS — Open source / self-host / BYO-agent: the Agents platform is a hosted SaaS; the docs describe Code tools running on 'ElevenLabs' infrastructure' and a hosted MCP server, and there is no self-host story — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/overview . The only 'bring your own' hook is Custom LLM: point the agent at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Chat Completions /v1/chat/completions or Responses /v1/responses, SSE with Content-Type: text/event-stream), and the agent's system tools are injected into the tools parameter of your requests — https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/llm/custom-llm.md . ElevenLabs explicitly recommends this pattern for putting an existing agent framework (LangGraph, Google ADK, CrewAI, LlamaIndex) behind its voice orchestration, translating the framework output into OpenAI-compatible SSE chunks — https://elevenlabs.io/blog/practical-guide-open-source-agent-frameworks-and-elevenagents . Its public SDK repos are open (e.g. elevenlabs-python, MIT) but the Agents platform itself is not — https://github.com/elevenlabs/elevenlabs-python .

ELEVENLABS — Pricing: billed by call minutes, not the shared credit pool. Plans: Free 15 min / 4 concurrent, Starter (75 min / 6), Creator (275 min / 10), Pro $99/mo (1,238 min / 20), Scale $299/mo (3,738 min / 30), Business $990/mo (12,375 min / 40). ElevenLabs hosting is $0.080/min included calls with $0.160/min burst and $0.003/text message; LLM and TTS/STT provider costs are separate ('based on usage and varies by model'); telephony is included at the same call-minute rate with no ElevenLabs telephony fee — https://elevenlabs.io/pricing/agents .

VAPI — Transports: SIP/telephony (SIP trunking with Twilio/Telnyx/Plivo/Zadarma/BYO, region-specific hosts sip.vapi.ai / sip.eu.vapi.ai, SIP REFER transfers) — https://docs.vapi.ai/advanced/sip/sip-trunk.mdx ; a dedicated WebSocket transport (transport.provider='vapi.websocket', PCM 16-bit 16kHz default or Mu-Law 8kHz, bidirectional binary audio + JSON control messages like {type:'hangup'}/{type:'end-call'}, auto sample-rate conversion) — https://docs.vapi.ai/calls/websocket-transport.mdx ; and WebRTC for browser/mobile 'via LiveKit/Daily' per the architecture page — https://docs.vapi.ai/security-and-privacy/data-flow.md . Client SDKs (web, React Native, Flutter, iOS) and server SDKs (TS/Python/Java/Ruby/C#/Go) are documented at https://docs.vapi.ai/quickstart/web.md . Call Listen is a separate unidirectional monitor-only WebSocket — https://docs.vapi.ai/calls/websocket-transport.mdx .

VAPI — Turn detection / VAD / interruption: StartSpeakingPlan controls when the assistant begins (waitSeconds default 0.4s; a Smart Endpointing Plan that is audio-based (Krisp, threshold 0-1 default 0.5), audio-text based (Deepgram Flux), LiveKit (English, with a customizable waitFunction like '200 + 8000 * x' mapping end-of-turn probability to ms), or Vapi's own model for non-English; or transcription-based endpointing via onPunctuationSeconds/onNoPunctuationSeconds/onNumberSeconds) — https://docs.vapi.ai/customization/speech-configuration.md and https://docs.vapi.ai/customization/voice-pipeline-configuration.md . StopSpeakingPlan controls when the assistant stops if the user talks (numWords before interrupting, voiceSeconds VAD default 0.2s, backoffSeconds before resuming default 1s); when numWords=0 the pipeline uses VAD instead of transcription — https://docs.vapi.ai/customization/speech-configuration.md . Custom endpointing is possible: Vapi POSTs call.endpointing.request (with messagesOpenAIFormatted) to assistant.startSpeakingPlan.smartEndpointingPlan.server.url and you reply {timeoutSeconds: X} — https://docs.vapi.ai/server-url/events.md . Critically, Vapi's Orchestration Layer (endpointing, interruption detection, background/voice filtering, backchanneling, emotion detection, filler injection) is 'Vapi proprietary ... not customizable and run on Vapi's infrastructure' — https://docs.vapi.ai/security-and-privacy/data-flow.md .

VAPI — Tools / webhooks: OpenAI-style tool/function calling; tools can ping your server — https://docs.vapi.ai/server-url/events.md . Tool types include API Request (direct HTTPS), Function (server webhook for tool-calls), built-in tools (transfer call, end call, SMS, DTMF keypad, API request), MCP servers, client-side tools handled entirely in the browser via the Web SDK, and a Query tool/custom knowledge base (your own retrieval server) — https://docs.vapi.ai/llms.txt (Tool/Integrations/Knowledge-base page titles) and https://docs.vapi.ai/tools/client-side-websdk.md . Advanced features include a tool rejection plan, static parameters as a prompt-injection boundary, variableExtractionPlan aliases to chain tool outputs, tool argument encryption, and dynamic bot_say messages — https://docs.vapi.ai/llms.txt . Server messages that expect a response are assistant-request, tool-calls, transfer-destination-request and knowledge-base-request; everything else is informational — https://docs.vapi.ai/server-url/events.md .

VAPI — Session state / context: a Call object plus an artifact bundle (recording, transcript, messages); a conversation-update server event carries the current conversation messages and messagesOpenAIFormatted — https://docs.vapi.ai/server-url/events.md . Chat sessions use previousChatId or sessionId for persistent context — https://docs.vapi.ai/llms.txt (Session management/Chat logs). Artifacts can be redirected to your own bucket (S3/GCP/R2/Azure/Supabase); orchestration data is ephemeral — https://docs.vapi.ai/security-and-privacy/data-flow.md .

VAPI — Transcript events (server-message schema): every message is POSTed as {message:{type:<server-message-type>, call:{...}, ...}} with common metadata (phoneNumber, timestamp, artifact, assistant, customer, call, chat). Transcript events: {type:'transcript', role:'user'|'assistant', transcriptType:'partial'|'final', transcript, originalTranscript, isFiltered, detectedThreats} (a final-only variant arrives as transcript[transcriptType="final"]); speech-update {status: started|stopped}; assistant.speechStarted {text (accumulating, not a delta), turn, timing{type:'word-alignment' (ElevenLabs) with words[] timestamps, or 'word-progress' (MiniMax with voice.subtitleType:'word')} — opt-in; conversation-update; user-interrupted {turnId} matching model-output turnIds so you can discard that turn; model-output; status-update; end-of-call-report {transcript, messages[]}; transfer-destination-request; transfer-update; language-change-detected; hang; knowledge-base-request; voice-input/voice-request; and call.endpointing.request — https://docs.vapi.ai/server-url/events.md .

VAPI — Handoff / multi-agent (Squads): Vapi has two primitives — Assistants (single prompt + tools) and Squads (multiple specialized assistants with context-preserving transfers) — https://docs.vapi.ai/quickstart/introduction . The Handoff tool transfers a call between assistants; destinations can be a specific assistant by id or name, an entire squad with a designated entry assistant, several options offered to the model, or resolved dynamically at runtime via the handoff-destination-request webhook; the receiving assistant's context is controlled by contextEngineeringPlan (e.g. {type:'lastNMessages', maxMessages:N} or full history) and structured data can be carried by a variableExtractionPlan; silent handoffs are supported; handoff attempts can be rejected by regex/Liquid/grouped conditions on conversation state; handoffs can also be triggered by assistant hooks on events like ending and speech interruptions — https://docs.vapi.ai/squads/handoff.md and https://docs.vapi.ai/llms.txt .

VAPI — Open source / self-host: closed-platform SaaS with open-source client/server SDKs (e.g. VapiAI/server-sdk-python). Bring-your-own-key/custom-server is supported for Transport, Transcriber, LLM and Voice, but the Orchestration layer (endpointing, interruption detection, emotion, backchanneling, filler) is Vapi-only and never customizable — https://docs.vapi.ai/security-and-privacy/data-flow.md . The FAQ states 'Yes, we support on-premise deployments for large Enterprises' but no technical self-host docs are published — https://docs.vapi.ai/faq.md . Pricing: $0.05/min Vapi hosting + model provider costs at cost ($0 if you bring your own provider key); 10 concurrent lines included then $10/line/mo; SMS/chat $0.005/msg; HIPAA add-on $2,000/mo; Zero Data Retention $1,000/mo; Scale tier is an annual contract — https://www.vapi.ai/pricing and https://docs.vapi.ai/enterprise/plans.md .

RETELL AI — Transports: custom telephony via SIP trunking (import numbers, bind agents, route SIP traffic) — https://docs.retellai.com/deploy/custom-telephony and https://docs.retellai.com/general/introduction.md ; a browser Web SDK (retell-client-js-sdk; your server calls create web call to mint an access_token valid 30s, the browser calls startCall({accessToken}), and the SDK exposes call state, live transcript and optional raw audio via emitRawAudioSamples) — https://docs.retellai.com/deploy/web-call.md ; a now-DEPRECATED raw bidirectional audio WebSocket wss://api.retellai.com/audio-websocket/{call_id} that streams mic audio bytes up and agent audio bytes down, with an optional enable_audio_alignment mode that returns base64 audio plus its text for captions — https://docs.retellai.com/api-references/audio-websocket ; provider WebSocket media-stream integrations (Twilio/Telnyx/Plivo/Exotel); and an outbound LLM WebSocket to your own server (see custom LLM below).

RETELL — Turn detection / VAD / interruption: turn-taking is platform-managed — Retell 'handles telephony, transcription, turn-taking, speech synthesis' and only asks your server for responses on its own schedule — https://docs.retellai.com/integrate-llm/overview.md . Tuning surface: audio preprocessing/denoising modes (No denoising | Remove noise (default) | Remove noise + background speech, which runs a background-voice-cancellation model and adds a $0.005/min surcharge) and an 'Interruption Sensitivity' knob (raise toward 0.8 to reduce false interruptions from background speech) — https://docs.retellai.com/build/handle-background-noise.md . Transcription mode trades latency for accuracy: 'optimize for speed' (interim results, low endpointing) vs 'optimize for accuracy' (higher endpointing, ~200ms extra) — https://docs.retellai.com/build/transcription-mode.md . In the custom-LLM protocol Retell can cancel an in-flight response by asking again with a new response_id, and your server can send an agent_interrupt message to make the agent speak immediately (cutting off whoever is talking and cancelling the in-flight response) — https://docs.retellai.com/integrate-llm/overview.md .

RETELL — Tools / function calling: function calling for single- and multi-prompt agents plus custom functions that call your API, integration tools (HubSpot, Salesforce, Dynamics 365, GoHighLevel, Zoho, Zendesk, Google Drive, OneDrive, Notion, Calendly, Cal.com), a Code tool (JavaScript), MCP tools (remote MCP servers), and conversation-flow function/MCP/subagent nodes — https://docs.retellai.com/llms.txt (function-calling.md, custom-function.md, integration-tools.md, code-tool.md, mcp.md). Built-ins include End Call (optionally with custom SIP headers), Transfer Call, Agent Transfer, Send SMS, Press Digit (DTMF/IVR), and Extract Dynamic Variable — https://docs.retellai.com/llms.txt . Webhook events delivered to your server: call_started, call_ended, call_analyzed, transcript_updated (voice) and equivalents for chat; 10s timeout with up to 3 retries; per-agent filtering via webhook_events — https://docs.retellai.com/features/webhook-overview.md .

RETELL — Session state / context: a Call object is the source of truth (same call_id across agent swaps, one history entry), plus call-level metadata, dynamic variables, contact memory across calls and SMS chats, post-call analysis/extraction, and configurable data retention/privacy controls — https://docs.retellai.com/build/single-multi-prompt/transfer-agent.md and https://docs.retellai.com/llms.txt . When you use a custom LLM, Retell explicitly warns you own latency/uptime/reconnection, that the LLM playground/simulation can't test it, that agent transfer cannot target a custom-LLM agent, and that your own tool calls only appear in the transcript if you report them yourself (Retell auto-records end_call/transfer_call/press_digit) — https://docs.retellai.com/integrate-llm/overview.md .

RETELL — Transcript events: the Monitor Call WebSocket streams a live transcript while the call runs (your app receives, never sends). Event types are transcript_snapshot (one event after admission, whole transcript so far), transcript_updated (one changed item each time; re-sent with the full text as a speaker keeps talking), and call_ended (then close code 1000, reason call_ended). Every transcript item has a stable id (role + per-role counter, e.g. agent_2) and is replaced by id, so reconnects are safe via a fresh snapshot. Item roles: user, agent, tool_call_invocation, tool_call_result, node_transition, dtmf, sms, injected; tool invocation items carry tool_call_id, tool name and a stringified-JSON arguments object; items carry time_sec but NOT per-word timing (fetch Get Call after the call for word timestamps) — https://docs.retellai.com/api-references/monitor-call-websocket.md .

RETELL — Handoff / multi-agent: the Agent Transfer tool (type agent_swap, with agent_id and optional agent_version) hands a live call from one AI agent to another on the SAME call/call_id; the destination inherits the full conversation history, call-level metadata, and dynamic variables; some call-level settings are pinned to the first agent while language/voice/LLM/prompt/tools/interruption sensitivity switch with the agent; swaps chain A->B->C and can transfer back; there is no fixed cap. It cannot target a custom-LLM-backed agent or a chat-channel agent. It is distinct from Call Transfer (to a human/external number, possibly via agentic warm transfer which places a real outbound call) — https://docs.retellai.com/build/single-multi-prompt/transfer-agent.md .

RETELL — Open source / self-host / pricing: closed hosted SaaS; open client SDKs (retell-client-js-sdk) and a TypeScript SDK, but no self-host documentation. Pricing starts at $0 pay-as-you-go with a $0.07-$0.31/minute range; Retell Voice Infra $0.055/min; platform voices $0.015/min; ElevenLabs v3 $0.10/min (Flash $0.040/min); LLM billed per minute (e.g. GPT 5.6 Terra $0.064/min); custom telephony is BYO ($0.00 telephony in the example) — https://www.retellai.com/pricing .

LIVEKIT AGENTS — Transports: WebRTC is the core (an SFU-based realtime platform; every client, agent and phone call joins a room as a participant publishing/subscribing to audio/video/data tracks) with client SDKs for web, Swift, Android, Flutter, React Native, Unity, Python, Node.js, Rust, C++, ESP32 — https://docs.livekit.io/llms.txt and https://docs.livekit.io/agents.md . Telephony is SIP via trunks + dispatch rules: SIP participants join rooms, SIP over UDP/TCP/TLS supported, RTP/SRTP supported, cold transfer (REFER) and warm transfer supported, SIP REGISTER and videoconference-over-SIP not supported; LiveKit Phone Numbers + LiveKit SIP are part of LiveKit Cloud, and self-hosted deployments must deploy the SIP service separately — https://docs.livekit.io/telephony.md . The server itself is open source and self-hostable on VMs/Kubernetes/multi-region — https://docs.livekit.io/transport.md and https://docs.livekit.io/transport/self-hosting/ . Realtime text/transcript data rides the same room as text streams and data messages rather than a separate JSON socket.

LIVEKIT — Turn detection / VAD / interruption: four detection modes — (1) the LiveKit turn detector model (default; audio+text end-of-turn prediction on top of VAD), (2) realtime models' own server-side detection (OpenAI Realtime / Gemini Live; set turn_detection='realtime_llm'; the model decides barge-in and the SDK rejects turn_handling.interruption.enabled=False with a ValueError), (3) VAD only (turn_detection='vad', for minimal latency or unsupported languages), (4) STT endpointing (turn_detection='stt', e.g. AssemblyAI/Deepgram Flux) — https://docs.livekit.io/agents/logic/turns.md . Silero VAD is a bundled plugin; adaptive interruption handling distinguishes true interruptions from backchanneling; endpointing is tunable with fixed min_delay/max_delay or dynamic endpointing — https://docs.livekit.io/agents/logic/turns.md .

LIVEKIT — Tools / function calling: function tools with a registration API, toolsets (add/remove groups), async tools for long-running work so the agent keeps talking, MCP servers, forwarding tool calls to the frontend via RPC, and guidance on tool-loop design under voice latency; prebuilt tools (EndCallTool, send_dtmf_events) and prebuilt tasks (GetName/GetEmail/GetAddress/GetDOB/GetPhoneNumber/GetCreditCard/GetDtmf/WarmTransferTask); LangChain/LangGraph integration is supported — https://docs.livekit.io/agents/llms.txt and https://docs.livekit.io/llms.txt .

LIVEKIT — Session state / context: AgentSession orchestrates the app and has explicit states (initializing -> starting -> running -> closing); documented events include agent_state_changed, user_state_changed (including an 'away' state after user_away_timeout, default 15s) and conversation_item_added; session commits user transcripts to history; there is session.userdata for arbitrary per-session state and a documented pattern for passing state; the room/participant model is the identity substrate — https://docs.livekit.io/agents/logic/sessions.md .

LIVEKIT — Transcript events (realtime transcript streaming): when the agent does STT in its pipeline, transcriptions are published to the frontend in realtime as a text stream on the lk.transcription topic, carrying an lk.transcribed_track_id attribute, with the sender identity being the transcribed participant; interim and final streams share the same segment_id and transcribed_track_id, and lk.transcription_final (true/false) distinguishes them — clients use registerTextStreamHandler and React's useTranscriptions hook (TranscriptionReceived and publish_transcription are deprecated). Agent speech text is published in sync with audio; a transcript can be TTS-aligned word-by-word (Cartesia/ElevenLabs/Rime support word-level timing; others sentence-level), and with json_format each chunk can be a JSON object with start_time/end_time per word; transcription_node + TimedString are available (experimental); text transforms (e.g. redaction) can be inserted — https://docs.livekit.io/agents/multimodality/text.md .

LIVEKIT — Handoff / multi-agent: an Agent defines instructions/tools/reasoning; the active agent can be changed with session.update_agent(...) or by RETURNING A DIFFERENT AGENT FROM A TOOL CALL (e.g. return BillingAgent(chat_ctx=self.chat_ctx), 'Transferring to billing'), which is the documented handoff mechanism — the LLM decides when to hand off. Workflows are modeled as agents + handoffs + tasks; there is a Supervisor pattern where a central agent routes work to specialist tasks while staying in control of the session — https://docs.livekit.io/agents/logic/agents-handoffs.md , https://docs.livekit.io/agents/logic/workflows.md and https://docs.livekit.io/agents/logic/patterns/supervisor.md . Because every agent is a room participant with an identity, 'who authored this utterance' is a first-class property (transcript sender identity = transcribed participant) — https://docs.livekit.io/agents/multimodality/text.md .

LIVEKIT — Open source / self-host / pricing: fully open source under Apache 2.0 (framework + ecosystem) — https://docs.livekit.io/agents.md and https://github.com/livekit/agents . The LiveKit server is an open-source WebRTC SFU that can be self-hosted (local, VMs, Kubernetes, multi-region) or run on LiveKit Cloud; the docs give an explicit self-hosted-vs-Cloud comparison where managed agent hosting and built-in observability (transcripts/traces/session recordings) are Cloud-only, and SIP must be deployed separately when self-hosting — https://docs.livekit.io/transport/self-hosting/ . Pricing: Free $0/mo, Ship $50/mo, Scale $500/mo; agents are metered by agent session minutes (e.g. ~$0.0100/min, with 1,000-5,000 minutes included depending on plan) plus transport/telephony lines itemised separately; self-hosting removes agent-hosting fees — https://livekit.io/pricing .

PIPECAT (Daily) — Transports: transports are modular and swappable without changing bot logic. Server-side transports include Daily (WebRTC), SmallWebRTC (direct P2P WebRTC, no cloud), LiveKit, FastAPI WebSocket, generic WebSocket, Media-over-QUIC, Vonage, WhatsApp, and various avatar transports — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/transports.md . Client SDKs (JavaScript, React, React Native, iOS, Android, C++) ship Daily WebRTC, SmallWebRTC, plain WebSocket, and — notably — direct OpenAI Realtime WebRTC and Gemini Live WebSocket transports — https://docs.pipecat.ai/llms.txt . Telephony runs over WebSocket with provider FrameSerializers (Twilio Media Streams, Telnyx, Plivo, Exotel) or Daily SIP/PSTN — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/transports.md and https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/telephony/overview.md (via index). Docs explicitly recommend WebRTC for client apps and WebSocket for server-to-server/telephony, citing TCP head-of-line blocking for WebSocket — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/transports.md .

PIPECAT — Turn detection / VAD / interruption: user turn strategies decide turn start (VAD via a local open-source Silero model, or transcription-based fallback) and turn end (Smart Turn model by default, SpeechTimeout strategy, an STT's own endpointing via external turn management, or Krisp VIVA) — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/speech-input.md . VAD is configured on the user aggregator via VADParams (confidence, start_secs, stop_secs, min_volume); VAD emits VADUserStartedSpeakingFrame/VADUserStoppedSpeakingFrame while the strategies emit UserStartedSpeakingFrame/UserStoppedSpeakingFrame — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/speech-input.md . Interruptions broadcast an InterruptionFrame (a SystemFrame handled immediately): every processor cancels work and discards queued data/control frames, the in-flight LLM completion is cancelled mid-stream (functions with cancel_on_interruption=True are cancelled and emit FunctionCallCancelFrame), TTS clears buffers, and the output transport flushes unplayed audio; only the words actually spoken are committed to context (observable via on_assistant_turn_stopped with an interrupted flag) — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/fundamentals/interruptions.md . Controls: AlwaysUserMuteStrategy/FirstSpeechUserMuteStrategy, MinWordsUserTurnStartStrategy, and disabling interruptions via VADUserTurnStartStrategy(enable_interruptions=False); for realtime speech-to-speech services the PROVIDER decides barge-in and Pipecat only flushes local audio — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/fundamentals/interruptions.md .

PIPECAT — Tools / function calling and RTVI control channel: function calling is via registered handlers (FunctionCallParams/result_callback) with per-tool cancel_on_interruption and cancellable_by_llm; an MCPClient connects MCP servers and registers their tools; filters/observers can gate frames — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/function-calling.md (via index) and https://docs.pipecat.ai/llms.txt . The RTVI protocol is the built-in client<->server control/messaging layer: RTVIProcessor (auto-added to each PipelineWorker, accessible as worker.rtvi) handles client-ready/version negotiation, services, actions and function-call notifications ('llm-function-call'), and any FrameProcessor can push an RTVIServerMessageFrame for unsolicited server-to-client data; RTVI can be disabled with enable_rtvi=False — https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/rtvi/rtvi-processor.md .

PIPECAT — Session state / context: LLMContext + LLMContextAggregatorPair are the conversation state; assistants/workers each own their own context; LLMContextSummarizer provides automatic context summarization; there is a documented 'Saving Conversation Transcripts' mechanism and an LLMTextProcessor for aggregating LLMTextFrames into logical units — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/context-management.md and https://docs.pipecat.ai/llms.txt .

PIPECAT — Transcript events: RTVI client callbacks deliver onUserTranscript/onBotTranscript with a TranscriptData payload carrying text and a boolean `final` flag (client code typically renders when data.final is true); the same events are available via RTVIEvent.UserTranscript etc. and React's useRTVIClientEvent; server-side observers (TranscriptionLogObserver, SpeakingObserver, TurnTrackingObserver, LLM/Tool observers) and turn events (on_assistant_turn_stopped) provide the server-side view; there are dedicated turn-management transcription and turn-events references — https://docs.pipecat.ai/client/concepts/events-and-callbacks.md , https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/utilities/turn-management/transcriptions.md and https://docs.pipecat.ai/llms.txt .

PIPECAT — Handoff / multi-agent / distinct authorship: Pipecat's multi-agent framework uses a main PipelineWorker that owns the transport and places a BusBridgeProcessor where an LLM would go; specialist LLMWorker agents are created bridged=() and start inactive (active=False). A handoff is a tool call that invokes activate_worker(target, args=..., deactivate_self=True), optionally injecting LLMWorkerActivationArgs messages into the target's context; the target's on_activated() fires and it responds. There is also job coordination (dispatch parallel work from one agent to others and collect results), distributed agents across processes/machines over the bus, and proxy agents across buses — https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/learn/agent-handoff.md and https://docs.pipecat.ai/llms.txt (multiple-llm-agents, job-coordination, distributed-agents, proxy-agents).

PIPECAT — Open source / self-host / pricing, and the direct GPT-Live hook: the framework is open source BSD 2-Clause (maintained by Daily and the community), and can be self-hosted or deployed to Pipecat Cloud; Pipecat Enterprise offers a self-hosted region with a split control/data plane — https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat and https://docs.pipecat.ai/overview/pipecat.md and https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat-cloud/enterprise/architecture.md (via index). Pricing is free for the framework; Pipecat Cloud agent profiles are $0.01/min (agent-1x, 0.5 vCPU/1GB), $0.02/min (agent-2x), $0.03/min (agent-3x), with integrated WebRTC $0.001 (free for 1:1 voice sessions), SIP $0.003-$0.02/min and PSTN $0.018/min — https://www.daily.co/pricing/pipecat-cloud/ .

PIPECAT IS THE CLOSEST EXISTING IMPLEMENTATION TO dsh-openai-live: OpenAILiveLLMService connects Pipecat to OpenAI's GPT-Live API using the gpt-live-1 model for full-duplex speech-to-speech — the model decides when to answer, stops when talked over, and delegates search/reasoning/tool work to a backend text model while the conversation continues; there is explicitly 'no client-side turn detection or response triggering'. Two delegation modes: ResponsesDelegation (OpenAI hosts the backend, configured via OpenAIResponsesLLMService.Settings with a model, and it uses the tools from your pipeline's LLMContext) and ClientDelegation (any Pipecat LLM service running in a BackendLLMWorker you provide, with its own LLMContext and tools). Delegation is not task-named: GPT-Live signals only that it is handing work over, the service sends the backend the transcript since the previous delegation, and each BackendOutput has a prefers_spoken flag controlling whether the model relays it (commentary) or keeps it as silent context. No local VAD, ExternalUserTurnStrategies(enable_interruptions=False), no InterruptionFrame broadcast (so every tool behaves as cancel_on_interruption=False unless you opt into cancellable_by_llm=True), session starts on the first LLMContextFrame/LLMRunFrame with at most 128 seeded messages and tool calls/results skipped from startup history, and set_messages + reset_conversation restores a saved conversation — https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/services/s2s/openai-live.md .

PIPECAT for coding agents specifically: Pipecat already ships an OpenClawGatewayService that drives an OpenClaw coding agent from a pipeline (start, steer, …) and a UIWorker that lets a voice agent read and act on a client GUI, plus classifiers and a 'Multiple LLM Agents' pattern where each agent owns its own LLM, tools and context — https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/services/agents/openclaw.md and https://docs.pipecat.ai/llms.txt . These are directly analogous to making voice a layer over a coding harness.

TRANSCRIPT-EVENT SCHEMA COMPARISON (for schema reuse): ElevenLabs = JSON events with nested *event objects, finalised user transcript only, char-level audio alignment, and agent_response_correction on interruption; Vapi = {message:{type,...}} with partial+final transcript entries and opt-in word-level timing, speech-update, and user-interrupted{turnId}; Retell = snapshot/updated/ended with replace-by-id items keyed by role+counter and time_sec; LiveKit = text streams on lk.transcription with lk.transcription_final, shared segment_id, sender identity and optional TTS-aligned per-word JSON; Pipecat RTVI = {text, final} with turn/lifecycle events and an observer pattern server-side. A coding harness that wants incremental captions plus a reconciliation signal should copy the final/interim + stable-item-id pattern (Retell/LiveKit) and an explicit 'spoken-so-far committed on interruption' contract (Pipecat/Vapi).
reuse_vs_reimplement: REUSE — Media transport, do not build it. For browser/first-party clients, reuse WebRTC via LiveKit (open source, self-hostable) or Pipecat's SmallWebRTC/Daily/LiveKit transports; for server-side audio, reuse a plain WebSocket transport (Pipecat's FastAPI/WebSocket transport or Vapi's vapi.websocket pattern of PCM/mu-law binary audio + JSON control frames). Telephony should only be added by reusing LiveKit SIP or Pipecat's Twilio/Telnyx/Plivo serializers. None of that logic is domain-specific to a coding harness.

REUSE — Turn detection/VAD only where it is not already the model's job. Because dsh-openai-live runs on GPT-Live full-duplex (the model self-detects turns and interruption, per Pipecat's OpenAILiveLLMService notes: 'No local VAD: the model detects the user's turns itself'), do NOT reuse a platform turn detector in the voice path. Reuse only a local VAD (open-source Silero, as bundled by both LiveKit and Pipecat) for optional UI affordances (speaking indicator, caption timing) — never as the turn decision. If a cascaded STT-LLM-TTS fallback path is ever needed, reuse proven end-of-turn models (LiveKit turn detector, Pipecat Smart Turn) rather than training your own.

REUSE — Barge-in/interruption semantics, reimplement only the local effects. Copy Pipecat's InterruptionFrame contract — on interruption cancel in-flight generation, drop queued TTS, flush the transport's unplayed audio, and commit only the words actually spoken to the context (with an interrupted flag). With GPT-Live the barge-in DECISION is the provider's, so reuse just this 'flush + commit spoken-so-far' behaviour and do not add a second barge-in detector (which would double-interrupt).

REUSE — Tool-calling envelope and cancellation semantics; keep your own executor. Adopt OpenAI-style function/tool schemas and per-tool cancellation metadata (Pipecat's cancel_on_interruption/cancellable_by_llm). But do NOT reuse any platform's tool registry as the authority: the harness's own agent loop owns tools. Expose the harness's tools to the voice layer through the GPT-Live delegation model (Pipecat's ResponsesDelegation, where the backend model calls your registered functions, maps almost exactly to 'voice hears, harness acts').

REUSE — Handoff-as-a-tool-call + an explicit context-carry policy. Every platform converges on the same shape: a handoff is a tool call (ElevenLabs transfer_to_agent, Vapi handoff tool, Retell agent_swap, LiveKit returning an Agent from a tool, Pipecat activate_worker(deactivate_self=True)). Reuse that convention plus the explicit context policy vocabulary (Vapi contextEngineeringPlan lastNMessages, Retell 'full history + metadata + dynamic variables') instead of inventing a control plane. For the coding session, reuse 'handoff preserves the transcript and carries a structured summary/variables forward' so the voice producer and the code producer see the same session.

REUSE — Author-identity conventions for a distinct producer. LiveKit models every agent as a room participant and tags transcriptions with the sender identity of the transcribed participant; Pipecat models each LLM agent as its own worker with its own LLM/context/tools. Copy that: emit transcript/session items with an explicit author field (livekit 'sender identity' style) and treat a handoff as a boundary. Note that ElevenLabs does NOT put agent_id on messages and instead uses the transfer tool call as a boundary marker — so if you integrate with a platform that lacks an author field, you must synthesise authorship yourself.

REUSE — Transcript streaming schema shape, not a specific platform's JSON. Reuse the final/interim + stable-item-id pattern (Retell transcript_snapshot/transcript_updated with replace-by-id; LiveKit lk.transcription_final + shared segment_id) and the {text, final} simplicity of Pipecat's RTVI UserTranscript/BotTranscript events. Reimplement the actual message names/transport bindings for DSH, but keep the semantics (idempotent item ids, interim vs final flag, monotonic ordering, reconciliation on reconnect) so any client can render and any reconnect can heal.

REUSE — Observability/evals scaffolding. Pipecat's observer pattern (Transcription/Speaking/TurnTracking/FunctionCall/LLM observers) and OpenTelemetry export, and LiveKit's data hooks/OpenTelemetry trace export, are proven shapes to copy for a voice session trace that joins the coding session trace.

REIMPLEMENT — The agent loop and orchestration. Do not put a third-party orchestration layer in the middle: Vapi's orchestration layer (endpointing, interruption detection, emotion, backchanneling, filler) is explicitly proprietary and non-customisable; ElevenLabs' turn-taking model always decides turn end (custom LLM only swaps the LLM, not the turn model); Retell manages turn-taking and only asks your server for responses. dsh-openai-live must own the loop and use GPT-Live + the harness as its brain.

REIMPLEMENT — Session/context ownership and the source of truth. These platforms own conversation history server-side (ElevenLabs conversations store, Vapi artifacts/call object, Retell Call object). For a coding session the harness's session log must be authoritative; mirror only a lightweight voice transcript into it. Do not let a platform transcript store become the canonical record of what the coding agent did.

REIMPLEMENT — Identity/tenancy/auth. Do not adopt a platform's agent/user/workspace model. Bind voice sessions to the harness's session id and map a platform participant/agent id only as an alias; own authentication yourself (ElevenLabs signed URLs / Retell server-minted access tokens are the reusable PATTERN, not the provider).

AVOID (if possible) — Closed, metered platforms for the voice path. ElevenLabs, Vapi and Retell are closed SaaS metered per minute ($0.08/min ElevenLabs hosting; $0.05/min Vapi + provider; $0.07-$0.31/min Retell) whose turn detection cannot be replaced, so the coding session's voice path would be governed by a third-party turn model and pricing. If managed voice infrastructure is reused at all, prefer the open, self-hostable options (LiveKit Apache-2.0, Pipecat BSD-2-Clause) so the whole path can be owned.

PRIORITY PICK — If exactly one building block is reused, reuse Pipecat: it is BSD-2-Clause, self-hostable, has a first-class gpt-live-1 service (OpenAILiveLLMService) with a delegation model that already matches 'voice is I/O, the harness is the reasoner', ships the OpenAI Realtime and Realtime-WebRTC client transports, the RTVI transcript event contract, and an interruption contract — i.e. it covers VAD/turn/transport/barge-in/transcript/tool-call/handoff/observability without forcing its own agent loop. LiveKit is the runner-up when the requirement is a distinct participant identity and room-native media with SIP.
